body:
The Cholas and their geographical base

The Cholas were an important ruling dynasty of southern India. Their imperial power developed from the middle of the 9th century CE, with its principal base in the Kaveri river delta of present-day Tamil Nadu.

The Kaveri delta provided fertile agricultural land, numerous river channels and favourable conditions for rice cultivation. The agricultural wealth of this region helped sustain the Chola kingdom, its administration, military activities and extensive temple construction.

The Cholas became particularly powerful under Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I during the late 10th and early 11th centuries.

Vijayalaya and the emergence of Chola power

Before the rise of the imperial Cholas, the Muttaraiyar chiefly family controlled the Kaveri delta under the authority of the Pallava rulers of Kanchipuram.

Vijayalaya Chola, who belonged to an older Chola chiefly family associated with Uraiyur, captured the Kaveri delta from the Muttaraiyar during the middle of the 9th century. He established Thanjavur as an important Chola centre.

His successors expanded the kingdom by conquering neighbouring territories, including lands previously controlled by the Pallavas and Pandyas. This expansion established the territorial foundation of the powerful Chola state.

Rajaraja I: expansion and administration

Rajaraja I became king in 985 CE. He greatly expanded Chola authority and reorganised the administration of the kingdom.

Rajaraja I is especially associated with the construction of the monumental Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, also known as the Brihadeshwara or Rajarajeswara Temple. The temple was completed and consecrated around 1009-1010 CE.

His reign is therefore remembered for military expansion, administrative consolidation and monumental temple architecture.

Rajendra I: northern and overseas expeditions

Rajendra I, the son and successor of Rajaraja I, continued the expansion of Chola power. His campaigns reached the Ganga valley, while Chola operations also extended to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

Rajendra I established Gangaikondacholapuram as a new imperial capital to commemorate his successful northern expedition. Its name means the city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga.

He also built a great Shiva temple at Gangaikondacholapuram, completed around 1035 CE.

In 1025 CE, Rajendra I launched a major naval expedition against the Srivijaya maritime kingdom in Southeast Asia. This expedition demonstrated the capacity of the Cholas to conduct military operations across the Bay of Bengal.

Rajaraja I: Administrative consolidation, territorial expansion and the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur.

Rajendra I: Ganga expedition, overseas naval campaigns and the new capital at Gangaikondacholapuram.

Prelims focus

  • Vijayalaya captured the Kaveri delta from the Muttaraiyar in the middle of the 9th century.
  • Uraiyur was associated with the earlier Chola chiefly family; Thanjavur became an important centre under Vijayalaya.
  • Rajaraja I became king in 985 CE and reorganised Chola administration.
  • Rajendra I conducted expeditions towards the Ganga valley, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
  • Rajendra I led the major naval expedition against Srivijaya in 1025 CE.
  • Trap: The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja I, while the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram was built by Rajendra I.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 22-24; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples, Brief Synthesis, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Great Living Chola Temples, monument descriptions, consulted 18 November 2026; Hermann Kulke, The Naval Expeditions of the Cholas in the Context of Asian History, in Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa, Chapter 1 summary, Cambridge Core, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The Chola heartland and monumental temple construction.

title: The Rise of the Cholas: From the Kaveri Delta to Imperial Power

body:
Central authority and local administration

The Chola kingdom was ruled by a powerful monarchy, but important administrative responsibilities were also performed by local institutions.

The king exercised overall authority, while village assemblies, groups of villages and associations of landholders and merchants handled various local affairs. These institutions helped organise agricultural production, maintain local resources, collect revenue and administer justice.

The Chola system is particularly important for understanding local self-government in early medieval India. However, local participation was strongly influenced by landownership and social position, and the institutions operated within a monarchy.

Ur: the village assembly

Ur was a village assembly associated with ordinary peasant settlements, particularly villages of non-Brahmana landholders.

The spread of irrigated agriculture made many peasant settlements prosperous. These settlements required arrangements for managing land, water, cultivation and local obligations.

The ur represented an important institution through which village affairs could be organised. It was not identical to the sabha found in Brahmana land-grant settlements.

Nadu: a group of villages

Several villages formed a larger territorial unit called a nadu.

The nadu and village councils performed administrative functions that included collecting taxes and dispensing justice. The nadu therefore operated at a wider territorial level than an individual village assembly.

Wealthy peasants, particularly influential Vellala landholders, exercised considerable authority in the affairs of the nadu under the supervision of the Chola government.

Chola rulers also recognised influential landholders by granting them titles and important positions. This connected powerful local families with the central administration.

Sabha: the assembly of Brahmana landholders

Sabha was an assembly of prominent Brahmana landholders that managed the affairs of a Brahmana land-grant settlement, generally called a brahmadeya.

The Chola rulers and other donors granted land to Brahmanas. Such grants contributed to the growth of Brahmana settlements, especially in the Kaveri valley.

The sabha administered the affairs of these settlements. Its responsibilities could include irrigation works, gardens, temples and other local matters. Its decisions were sometimes recorded in inscriptions on temple walls.

The sabha was a more restricted landholding institution than the general village assembly. Membership and committee service were governed by qualifications, rather than participation by every adult resident.

Nagaram: the merchant association

A nagaram was an association of merchants in a town. Nagarams sometimes performed administrative functions connected with urban and commercial affairs.

The nagaram should not be confused with the ur or sabha, which were associated with village settlements.

Land categories and revenue

Agriculture was a major source of resources for the Chola kingdom. Land revenue helped support royal administration, military requirements, public works and temple construction.

Chola inscriptions identify different categories of land according to ownership or the purpose for which the land was granted.

Land categoryMeaning
VellanvagaiLand belonging to non-Brahmana peasant proprietors.
BrahmadeyaLand granted to Brahmanas.
DevadanaLand granted to temples.
ShalabhogaLand assigned for the maintenance of a school.

These categories describe the status or assigned purpose of land. They are not names of taxes.

Kadamai and vetti

Two particularly important terms connected with Chola taxation were kadamai and vetti.

  • Kadamai: Land revenue collected from agricultural land.
  • Vetti: Compulsory labour demanded as a form of taxation or obligation rather than payment in cash.

Chola inscriptions contain more than 400 terms relating to different taxes and dues. These included obligations connected with land and several other activities.

The distinction between kadamai and vetti is essential: land revenue and compulsory labour were not the same form of payment.

Understanding Chola local self-government

Local bodies could manage important village affairs, but their authority was not equivalent to modern democratic self-government. Landownership and social status affected participation, while the central Chola state continued to exercise supervision.

Prelims focus

  • Ur: Village assembly associated with ordinary peasant settlements.
  • Nadu: Larger administrative unit comprising several villages.
  • Sabha: Assembly of prominent Brahmana landholders in a brahmadeya settlement.
  • Nagaram: Association of merchants in a town.
  • Kadamai: Land revenue; vetti: Compulsory labour.
  • Trap: Ur, sabha and nagaram were not interchangeable names for one institution.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 18, 25-27; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6 History, Chapter 11, New Empires and Kingdoms, p. 117.]

pictures.alt: The Chola king supervised local institutions: nadu grouped villages with distinct ur and sabha assemblies, while nagaram was a town merchant association.
pictures.caption: Local institutions within the Chola kingdom.

title: Chola Local Administration: Ur, Nadu, Sabha and Land Revenue

body:
Uttaramerur and village administration

The Uttaramerur inscriptions from present-day Tamil Nadu provide important information about the organisation of local administration during the Chola period.

Uttaramerur was a Brahmana settlement with a sabha. The inscriptions explain how members were selected for committees that performed particular administrative duties.

The sabha did not perform every task through a single undivided body. Different committees were responsible for specific areas of village management.

Functions of sabha committees

The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe arrangements for committees concerned with matters such as:

  • Irrigation: Maintenance and management of tanks and other water-related works.
  • Gardens: Supervision of garden-related property and activities.
  • Temples: Management of matters associated with local temples.

Such committees made it possible to allocate responsibility for different village functions rather than leaving every administrative matter to the entire assembly.

Eligibility for committee membership

Membership was subject to qualifications. The Uttaramerur inscription described requirements concerning property, age, knowledge, conduct and previous committee service.

RequirementRule described in the inscription
LandownershipThe prospective member had to own land from which land revenue was collected.
ResidenceThe prospective member had to possess a home of his own.
AgeThe prescribed age range was 35-70 years.
KnowledgeKnowledge of the Vedas and competence in administrative matters were expected.
ConductHonesty was required.
Previous serviceA person who had served on a committee during the previous 3 years was ineligible for another committee.
AccountsA former committee member who failed to submit his accounts was disqualified, as were relatives including his brothers and sons.

These conditions show that committee membership was restricted to a qualified section of society. The process was not based on universal adult participation.

The pot-ticket method of selection

The selection procedure is commonly known as the kudavolai system, or pot-ticket method.

Under this procedure, names of eligible persons were written on small palm-leaf tickets. The tickets were placed in an earthenware pot. A young boy then drew the tickets, one by one, for the relevant committees.

The essential distinction is between eligibility and selection. Property, knowledge, age and conduct requirements determined who could be considered. Drawing tickets from a pot determined which eligible persons were selected.

This was therefore not the same as an election in which all adult residents voted to choose their preferred representatives.

Qualification came before selection

The use of a pot and palm-leaf tickets did not make committee membership open to everyone. Only persons who satisfied the applicable conditions could enter the selection process.

Prelims focus

  • Uttaramerur is associated with Chola-period sabha administration in Tamil Nadu.
  • The prescribed age range for committee membership was 35-70 years.
  • Landownership, possession of a home, knowledge of the Vedas and honest conduct were among the requirements.
  • Service on a committee during the previous 3 years was a disqualification for another committee.
  • Eligible names were written on palm-leaf tickets and drawn from an earthenware pot.
  • Trap: The pot-ticket method was selection by lot among eligible persons, not universal adult voting.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 26-27; NDTV, This Tamil Nadu Town Had World's Earliest Democracy Model, 30 November 2025, sections on the Kudavolai method and eligibility, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Eligibility rules come first; eligible names go on palm-leaf tickets into a pot, a young boy draws them, and selected persons serve on sabha committees.
pictures.caption: Uttaramerur committee-selection procedure.

title: The Uttaramerur Inscriptions and the Selection of Sabha Committees

body:
The agricultural importance of the Kaveri delta

The agricultural prosperity of the Kaveri delta was a major foundation of Chola power.

Before entering the Bay of Bengal, the Kaveri River divides into several channels. These channels distribute water across the delta and deposit fertile alluvial soil when they overflow.

The combination of water and fertile soil provided favourable conditions for agriculture, particularly rice cultivation.

Large-scale agriculture expanded in this region during the early medieval period. This expansion required more than the natural fertility of the soil. Land had to be prepared, and the movement of water had to be managed.

Preparing agricultural land

The development of cultivation involved several forms of work:

  • Clearing forests: Creating additional areas suitable for cultivation.
  • Levelling land: Preparing fields so that water could be distributed effectively.
  • Constructing embankments: Helping prevent excessive flooding in the delta.
  • Constructing canals: Carrying water from available sources towards cultivated fields.

These works converted potentially fertile land into agricultural areas that could be cultivated more reliably.

Major methods of irrigation

Natural river channels did not provide adequate or conveniently located water in every area. Farmers and local authorities therefore used several methods of artificial irrigation.

1. Irrigation tanks

Irrigation tanks were reservoirs constructed to collect and store water, especially rainwater.

Stored water could be released when required for cultivation. This was particularly useful where agricultural requirements could not be met by immediate rainfall or direct access to river channels.

2. Wells

In some areas, wells were dug to obtain water for irrigation.

Wells provided an additional source of water where underground water could be reached and used for agricultural purposes.

3. Canals and channels

Canals carried water towards fields. In the Kaveri delta, natural river branches and constructed channels together supported the distribution of water.

Canals had to be maintained so that water could continue to flow to the areas requiring it.

4. Embankments and sluice gates

Embankments helped regulate the spread of water and protect cultivated land from flooding.

A sluice gate regulated the release of water from a tank or another water channel. By controlling the opening through which water passed, the flow towards irrigation channels could be managed.

A 9th-century sluice gate from Tamil Nadu illustrates the use of this form of water control during the period.

How irrigation supported agricultural production

Reliable irrigation allowed cultivation to continue beyond the immediate availability of rainfall. In many areas of the Kaveri region, farmers could grow 2 crops in a year.

Greater agricultural production supported prosperous settlements and provided a larger base from which land revenue could be collected.

Who managed irrigation works?

Irrigation required collective organisation. Constructing a tank was only the beginning: channels had to be maintained, embankments repaired and the available water distributed.

Chola rulers and village communities both took an interest in these activities. Local institutions, including sabha committees concerned with irrigation, could supervise important water-management works.

Thus, irrigation was connected with both agricultural prosperity and local administration.

Do not confuse the Kaveri delta's natural river channels with constructed irrigation tanks. River channels carried flowing water, while tanks stored collected water for controlled use. Both contributed to cultivation.

Prelims focus

  • The Kaveri delta was the principal agricultural heartland of the imperial Cholas.
  • Rice was an important crop of the delta.
  • Tanks collected rainwater; wells and canals provided other irrigation arrangements.
  • Embankments helped manage flooding, while sluice gates regulated water release.
  • In many areas, irrigation supported cultivation of 2 crops annually.
  • Trap: Irrigation management was not performed exclusively by the king; village communities also participated.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 24-26, sections Agriculture and Irrigation and The Administration of the Empire; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Chapter 2, illustration and description of the 9th-century Tamil Nadu sluice gate, p. 25.]

title: Agriculture and Irrigation: Why the Kaveri Delta Was Important
